rationale: B wins because it turns the same announcement into more usable press inventory: a category story, a revenue-math story, a named-creator story, and a defensive writer story. A is strong, especially "Substack says its top creators made over $400M last year — but won't say who or how much each," but its funding angle leans on the mushy phrase "short on funding" and needs more scaffolding than it admits. B's "What Substack's $400M creator number says about Substack's own revenue" is the sharper reporter bait: it knows exactly what a skeptical business reporter will do with the numbers.
gaps_in_A: "Substack is spending on a media-app build while privately held and short on funding" overstates the supplied fact. The update says public funding struggles, not that Substack is currently short on funding.
"capital-intensive infrastructure" is a plausible inference, but it is still an inference. A flags the thinness later, but the angle headline/body sells it harder than the facts support.

"the same cut now extending over video and podcast monetization" is too confident. The facts say Substack takes 10% of subscription revenue; they do not prove identical economics for every new video or podcast use case.
gaps_in_B: "Substack is done being a newsletter company" is a little too absolute. The facts support a media-app push, not a completed identity change.
"the next chapter of a story the press is already telling" imports outside coverage texture. Public funding struggles are supplied; a current press narrative is not.

"the moment writers see video in their subscribers' feeds" gets ahead of the update. A TikTok-style feed is supplied, but subscriber-feed behavior and ranking effects need proof before they become copy.
